node.label: Liang Qichao
node.date_label: An Introduction to Chinese History (1901) · New Historiography (Xin shixue) (1902) · Observations on a Trip to America (1903) · Outline of Scholarship in the Qing Dynasty (1920) · Nankai lectures on methods of Chinese historical research (1921)
node.description: A reform-era Chinese scholar whose historiographical programme moved beyond dynastic court narratives toward histories of people and social change. Civic renewal in his authorized translated text combines inherited resources with selective borrowing. Blitstein shows that Liang’s 1920 account of Qing scholarship recovered a Chinese intellectual renewal, while Hu Shi used renaissance differently. Dirlik credits Liang’s break with older historical writing but questions its explanatory framework. These shifts prevent treating his lifetime’s work as one unchanging nationalist doctrine.
node.representative_figures_and_works: An Introduction to Chinese History (1901); New Historiography/Xin shixue (1902); Renewing the People (selected translated text); Observations on a Trip to America (1903); Outline of Scholarship in the Qing Dynasty/Qingdai xueshu gailun (written 1920); Nankai historical-method lectures (1921).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: authorized Columbia translations of selected writings; Dirlik’s introduction and epilogue passages; Blitstein pp. 180–182; Zheng’s relevant historical discussion. The 1902 and 1920 works are known through named academic readers, not newly read in Chinese. The 1921 milestone dates lectures, without conflating them with later editions of Chinese historical research methods. Blitstein’s 2021 issue date is distinct from 2020 online/copyright metadata. No direct relation to individual European thinkers is inferred from resemblance.

incident_edges.relationship: History beyond dynastic courts, joined to civic and national renewal (1901–1903)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Dirlik’s epilogue discusses Liang’s 1902 programme; the authorized Renewing the People excerpt describes renewal as a selective combination of inherited and acquired resources. Zheng traces the changing national vocabulary. This does not equate civic renewal with one fixed ethnic nationalism.
incident_edges.map_label: History beyond dynastic courts, joined to civic and national renewal (1901–1903)

incident_edges.relationship: Qing scholarship reinterpreted as a Chinese renaissance (1920), in Blitstein’s reading
incident_edges.evidence_note: Blitstein, pp. 180–182, contrasts Liang’s recovery of the Qing intellectual past with Hu Shi’s future-oriented renaissance. The statement is mediated by this named reader; no universal equation between Chinese and European histories follows.
incident_edges.map_label: Qing scholarship reinterpreted as a Chinese renaissance (1920), in Blitstein’s reading

incident_edges.relationship: Dirlik credits the break with inherited historiography but questions its comprehensive explanatory framework (1978)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Dirlik’s introduction, pp. 3–4, argues that Liang’s and Gu’s innovations did not supply a replacement general theory; the epilogue distinguishes social history and document criticism. This is Dirlik’s appraisal routed through Marxist historiography, not a collective rejection of Liang.

records.context: Recast historical writing around people, society and civic renewal in early-twentieth-century China; the forms of nationhood changed across his work.
records.works: New Historiography (1902; through Dirlik); Renewing the People (authorized translated excerpt)

records.context: Reinterpreted Qing learning in 1920 as an internally significant intellectual renewal; Blitstein distinguishes this from Hu Shi’s programme.
